Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimant, XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX, seeks refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (the IRPA).1
The claimant's identity has been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2 ALLEGATIONS

The claimant fears a businessman named XXXXX and his brother XXXXX, an employee of the XXXXX XXXXX XXXXX. The claimant alleges that he operated a XXXXX XXXXX in XXXXX in the state of Mexico from 1998 to 2008. XXXXX, who owned a similar store across the street from the claimant's and was a business competitor, attempted to coerce the claimant's customers to shop at his store and the claimant's employees to work for him. XXXXX physically assaulted XXXXX, the claimant's employee, in 2004. Shots were fired at the claimant's store on the evenings of XXXXX, 2004 and XXXXX, 2004. A security guard witnessed XXXXX van leaving the scene following both shooting incidents. The claimant was visited by XXXXX brother XXXXX who threatened the claimant to not report anything to the police and for the claimant to move away or he and his brother XXXXX would take care of the matter themselves. In XXXXX 2005, XXXXX and XXXXX threatened the claimant at the claimant's house. XXXXX and XXXXX, both Catholics, told the claimant to close his business and abandon his religious following as a Jehovah Witness. XXXXX fired gun shots at the claimant's house before he and Juan left. In late 2005 or early 2006, XXXXX attempted to assault the claimant at the claimant's store and fired shots at the claimant's store after the claimant ran inside the store to get away from XXXXX. Shortly afterwards, XXXXX and two police officers physically assaulted and attempted to arrest the claimant. XXXXX and the two police officers left without the claimant after some neighbours questioned the police about the reason for the claimant's arrest.

In XXXXX or XXXXX 2006, the claimant went to reside in Mexico City. While in Mexico City, XXXXX, XXXXX and two police officers shot through the door and window of the house the claimant was staying in. On XXXXX, 2007, XXXXX attempted to hit the claimant with his vehicle. In XXXXX 2008, the claimant moved to XXXXX. Shortly after moving to XXXXX, XXXXX crashed through the main door of the house with his truck. The claimant fled Mexico on XXXXX, 2008 and filed a claim for refugee protection on June 11, 2008.

I find that the claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. The claimant does not have a well-founded fear of persecution for a Convention reason and his removal to Mexico would not subject him personally to a risk to life, or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a danger of torture.

In arriving at my decision, I considered the issue of whether the claimant's fear is objectively reasonable as it relates to section 96 and as it relates to section 97 of the IRPA. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether or not the claimant took all reasonable steps to avail himself of that protection, and whether he has provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. ANALYSIS State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. In this regard, the courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. A claimant can rebut this presumption by providing clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3 The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.4

No state is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times and the fact that the state is not always successful in protecting its citizens is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.5

Furthermore, the law states that the burden for the claimant to prove an absence of state protection is directly proportional to the level of democracy in that state. In a functioning democracy, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus on the claimant to show he or she has exhausted all courses of action reasonably available to them.6 Moreover, local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.7

The documentary evidence8 before the Board indicates that Mexico is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Having canvassed the country conditions documents,9 I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There is nothing in the documentary evidence before the Board to suggest that Mexico is in a state of complete breakdown.

Furthermore, the Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical, and a complainant can seek redress at a higher level if dissatisfied with the services at the local level.10 According to the documentary evidence11, there are a number of authorities and agencies who will assist members of the public if they believe they have encountered a corrupt official or if they are not satisfied with the services of the security forces.

There is documentary evidence12 that persons who face police misconduct, inefficiency or corruption can ask the Secretariat of the Public Administration (SFP), the Program Against Impunity, or the Office of the Attorney General (PGR) to investigate federal and state police failures or misconduct.

Further documentary evidence indicates that persons seeking redress from corrupt or complicit officials can do so through the National or State Human Rights Commissions and the General Comptroller's Assistance Directorate.13

It is noted that transgressors on the security forces face sanctions, removal, suspension or dismissal.14 In addition, the Federal Agency of Investigation (AFI) deals with corrupt state officials, drug traffickers and kidnappers.15

Documentary evidence16 indicates that efforts to ensure police effectiveness and purge corruption include investigations by the Secretary of Public Security, complaints monitored by the Inspector General, and a 24-hour hotline to report corrupt officials.

Further documentary evidence17 indicates that the security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and certification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers, including arrests, prosecutions and convictions of members of the security forces. The new government laws attacking corruption and bribery have resulted in sentences of five to ten years' imprisonment for convicted officials, which have reportedly had a marked effect.18

In this particular case, the claimant was questioned as to what efforts he made to seek state protection before fleeing Mexico. The claimant went to the police shortly after he began having problems with XXXXX. The police recommended that the claimant avoid XXXXX. The claimant reported to the police the threats he received from XXXXX and the two shooting incidents that occurred in XXXXX 2004. The police told the claimant that they would speak with XXXXX after the holidays. The police later asked the claimant for photographs of the bullet holes. When the claimant followed up with the police, they told the claimant that XXXXX threats were considered matters of conciliation.

XXXXX assault of XXXXX, the claimant's employee, was reported to the Public Ministry by XXXXX, XXXXX father and the claimant after XXXXX was released from hospital. XXXXX proposed and XXXXX father agreed to an arrangement where XXXXX would pay for damages, XXXXX medical expenses and XXXXX lost wages to avoid prosecution.

The claimant testified that he reported the XXXXX 2005 shooting incident to the police. XXXXX was apprehended and detained for two days. The attorney general's office initiated an investigative proceeding for XXXXX attempted homicide of the claimant that was held from XXXXX to XXXXX 2005. Following the proceeding, the court determined that there was insufficient evidence to proceed with a criminal trial.

The claimant testified that he witnessed XXXXX, XXXXX and the two police officers being placed into a police car of the Federal District following the 2006 shooting incident in Mexico City. The claimant was unable to determine what action was taken against the four men involved in the shooting as the claimant left the scene shortly after the men were placed in the police car.

On XXXXX, 2007 the claimant filed a denunciation with the state attorney general's office against XXXXX for attempting to run the claimant over with his vehicle a day prior. The state official told the claimant that the denunciation was only a statement of facts and that the statement would be sent to the Public Ministry office to determine if an investigation was warranted. The claimant did not follow up with the state attorney general's office or the Public Ministry because he did not believe the police were paying attention to his denunciations.

I find that the claimant received police attention every time the claimant approached the authorities. There is no information to suggest that the police were not making genuine and earnest efforts to investigate the claimant's allegations and apprehend the claimant's perpetrators if warranted.

Claimants are required to show that they sought all avenues of protection reasonably available before seeking international protection.19 In this particular case, the claimant did not report all the threats, assaults and shooting incidents to the police prior to fleeing Mexico. On the occasions he did file a report, he received attention; investigations were conducted and criminal proceedings were held. It would be unreasonable to expect the authorities to act effectively if they do not have information on all related matters. The panel is of the opinion that the claimant ought to have shown that he had taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek state protection in Mexico before seeking international protection in Canada.

Further, I considered the claimant's efforts to report any of this information to any other authority and find that he did not do so. When asked if he considered reporting the threats, assaults and shootings to any other authority, the claimant indicated that the police determine which jurisdiction handles each type of crime and that the crimes were state crimes and that there are no other venues to go to. I find that if the claimant was dissatisfied with the services at the local level, he could have sought redress at a higher level as the Mexican security forces are described as hierarchical.20 Therefore, I find that the claimant simply did not reasonably exhaust courses of action open to him to obtain state protection in Mexico, and hence, he has not discharged the onus of showing clear and convincing proof of the state's inability or unwillingness to protect him.

The panel has considered the documentary evidence21 submitted by counsel with respect to state protection in Mexico. The Houston Chronicle article22 entitled "Mexico's 'FBI' investigates 1,493 agents" reports that 1,493 members of the Federal Investigation Agency (AFI) are under investigation for probably committing crimes and that 457 of those currently face prosecution. The article23 entitled "Police Forces in Mexico: A Profile" describes Mexico's complex variety of police forces with different functions and jurisdictions. Under the heading Crime and Public Security, the article states that according to official data (INEGI) in 2001 there were 24,742 sentenced criminals and 28,619 people charged in the federal jurisdiction and 123,071 sentenced criminals and 163,995 people charged in local crimes. In Judith Adler Hellman's "Report on Human Rights in Mexico"24, the author makes statements such as "Mexicans have no recourse to the police for protection from wrongdoers as we do in Canada" and "It basically makes no sense to call on the police to rescue oneself from harm". I find that the author makes general sweeping statements regarding state protection in Mexico with little empirical data to back up her findings. Although the majority of the articles contained in counsel's documentary evidence report on crime and corruption in Mexico, Mexico's efforts to combat crime and curb corruption are often contained in the same articles.

The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence25; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious and genuine efforts to address the problem of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I am of the view, in perusing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico.

I find that the claimant, in the circumstances of this case, has failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimant seek it.

For all these reasons, I find that the claim cannot succeed. There is no objective basis for the claimant's alleged fear, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the IRPA, as adequate state protection is available to him.

The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects his claim. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
